trust_policy.page.launch_body: Trust grows faster when coverage is dense and predictable. YardMatch is intentionally prioritizing the launch radius before broad expansion.
trust_policy.page.why_body: YardMatch is meant to be a managed marketplace, so the public promise about support, legal basics, booking rules, and provider expectations should match how the product and ops flow actually behave.
trust_policy.booking_expectations.descri: Understand the recommendation-first booking flow, limited backup options, arrival expectations, and what YardMatch manages after a booking is requested.
trust_policy.booking_expectations.sectio: The core customer flow is recommendation-first: choose the service, timing, and property, then confirm the best-fit provider quickly unless you need a small backup list for trust.
Open-ended provider browsing is not the default launch flow.
Alternative providers are meant to stay curated and limited.
Pricing and booking context should feel managed rather than chaotic.
A booking request should move into a managed follow-through flow instead of leaving the customer unsure about who is arriving or what the next step is.
Providers confirm bookings before route and work-start actions continue.
Arrival tracking should reflect the provider route status, not expose individual crew location unnecessarily.
Recurring plans should keep future visits intentional instead of feeling like accidental repeat orders.
Support, disputes, and refund reviews are part of the product promise, not an afterthought bolted on after booking.
Customers should have a clear support path if timing, quality, or billing becomes a problem.
Ops can intervene, document decisions, and reconcile financial consequences when needed.
Trust comes from both the recommendation and what happens after the booking is placed.
trust_policy.booking_expectations.summar: YardMatch is designed to recommend one best-fit provider first, with a limited backup path for trust, not an open-ended directory experience.
trust_policy.booking_expectations.title: What to expect when you book
trust_policy.cancellation_policy.descrip: Learn how YardMatch handles customer cancellations, reschedules, provider delays, and low-supply schedule changes during launch.
trust_policy.cancellation_policy.section: Customers should be able to cancel or reschedule future requested bookings while the booking is still operationally safe to change.
Requested bookings can be cancelled from the customer flow.
Future bookings can be rescheduled when the provider window remains available.
Address changes are allowed only while the booking state and route conditions still permit them.
When the business owner or ops needs to move a booking, the change should be visible, justified, and communicated instead of being treated like silent back-office churn.
Provider and ops reschedules should leave an intervention trail.
Late updates and exception handling should notify the customer when the flow supports it.
Recurring plans should cancel future requested visits cleanly when the plan is ended.
During launch, coverage is intentionally narrow and local, so weather, route density, and supply constraints may still force occasional schedule changes.
Dense local coverage is preferred over overpromising broad availability.
Low-supply days should be handled with clear follow-up, not ambiguous silence.
The public promise should stay aligned with what ops can actually fulfill.

trust_policy.privacy_policy.section.1.bu: Customer contact, address, and property details support booking, routing, and service delivery.
Provider and crew identity details support staffing, work records, notifications, and accountability.

trust_policy.privacy_policy.section.2.bo: The launch product should stay disciplined about collecting data only when it supports a real marketplace need instead of hoarding information for vague future ideas.
trust_policy.privacy_policy.section.2.bu: Public attribution is privacy-safe and avoids logging raw personal URLs.
Anonymous location lookup stays session-scoped unless there is a stronger product reason to save it.
Property and service photos stay private booking evidence by default. Public before-and-after use requires the customer's explicit, revocable permission and excludes their name and street address.
trust_policy.privacy_policy.section.3.bo: Some marketplace data is retained because support, disputes, evidence review, and payouts require an audit trail after the booking is placed.
trust_policy.privacy_policy.section.3.bu: Support tickets, before-and-after evidence, and financial-exception workflows may require stored history that is visible only to authorized booking participants and operations.
Launch leads are tracked so follow-up and conversion handling do not disappear into ad hoc inboxes.
Policy language should stay aligned with the actual product behavior and stored operational records.
trust_policy.privacy_policy.summary: YardMatch uses customer, provider, and crew information to run marketplace operations, but the public flow should avoid collecting more personal data than launch operations actually need.

trust_policy.provider_standards.descript: See the service-quality, verification, support, and communication expectations YardMatch intends to hold landscaping businesses to during launch.
A provider should only expose capacity the business can realistically service and should keep its marketplace profile, calendar, and service area aligned with field reality.
Verification should happen before a provider is shown publicly.
Service radius and availability settings should reflect real operating capacity.
Growth should not come from accepting work that crews, routes, or pricing cannot support.
YardMatch expects providers to treat route windows, communications, and documentation seriously because those behaviors shape trust more than marketing copy does.
Bookings should be confirmed before route and work-start actions continue.
Before and after evidence, notes, or checklists may be required by the live ops flow.
Late updates, exceptions, and reschedules should be communicated instead of hidden.
Reviews, disputes, billing questions, and support escalations are part of provider quality, not something outside the marketplace relationship.
Providers should participate in service-quality and refund-review follow-up when needed.
Dispute evidence and support actions can affect payouts until the case is resolved.
Long-term marketplace trust depends on fulfillment quality, not only on lead volume.
trust_policy.provider_standards.summary: Providers are expected to confirm work they can actually fulfill, communicate clearly, respect route commitments, and participate in support or refund review when a job goes sideways.
trust_policy.provider_standards.title: Provider standards and launch expectations
trust_policy.provider_verification.descr: Understand the launch-era verification expectations behind the recommendation-first marketplace, including what is reviewed before a landscaping business is surfaced publicly.
trust_policy.provider_verification.secti: A recommendation-first marketplace only works if the customer can trust that the providers being surfaced are real businesses with enough operational readiness to fulfill the work.
Public marketplace overview routes are intended to show verified providers only.
Verification is part of the trust layer, not an optional cosmetic badge.
The point is to reduce false confidence from thin profiles or unreviewed supply.
The exact checklist can evolve, but the launch posture is to review whether a provider looks operationally ready for the service area, booking flow, and support expectations being promised publicly.
Service area, category fit, and route reality should match what the provider is listing.
Calendar and availability controls should not expose impossible booking windows.
Support, review, payout, and dispute expectations should be acceptable before public launch demand is routed to that business.
What YardMatch is checking at launch

Verification does not guarantee a perfect job, but it does mean YardMatch is trying to filter public demand through a narrower, more accountable set of providers than a generic listing directory would.
Customers still get support, refund-review, and dispute paths if something goes wrong.
Verification works together with review, punctuality, and follow-through data over time.
As real local performance data grows, trust should be based on both screening and operating history.
trust_policy.provider_verification.summa: YardMatch aims to show only verified providers in the public marketplace overview, so launch trust is based on screening and operational fit instead of directory sprawl alone.

trust_policy.refund_policy.section.1.bod: Refunds are reviewed in context instead of being treated like an immediate one-click reversal after every completed job.
trust_policy.refund_policy.section.1.bul: Customers can request a refund review from completed paid bookings.
A billing support ticket is created automatically when that review path opens.

trust_policy.refund_policy.section.2.bod: When a case includes submitted evidence, ops should review that material before choosing a direction, and the final decision should match the reviewed signal.
trust_policy.refund_policy.section.2.bul: Support evidence can include before and after photos, notes, and checklists.
High-stakes resolutions should not bypass reviewed evidence.
Mixed or inconclusive evidence requires a more specific manual rationale.
trust_policy.refund_policy.section.3.bod: Because this is a managed marketplace, payment and payout state can be held while service-quality or billing issues are being resolved.
trust_policy.refund_policy.section.3.bul: Refund-review and dispute cases can place payouts on hold.
Disputed bookings freeze settlement until support resolves the case.
When Stripe is configured, approved refunds are expected to sync back to the processor path as well.

trust_policy.terms_of_service.descriptio: Understand the launch-era ground rules for using YardMatch, including managed booking expectations, support boundaries, and route-window realities.
YardMatch is not a generic lead directory. The product is designed to recommend a best-fit provider, manage the booking flow, and stay involved when support or payment issues appear.
Recommendation-first booking is the intended default experience.
Limited backup options exist for trust, not for open-ended comparison shopping.
Support, billing, and dispute handling are part of the marketplace promise.
Coverage, timing, route windows, weather, and labor supply can all affect how quickly a job can be fulfilled, especially during a narrow launch radius.
Route windows are operational commitments, not minute-by-minute guarantees.
Cancellations, delays, and reschedules should be handled transparently rather than silently.
The launch area should stay dense and manageable instead of overpromising thin regional coverage.
Using the marketplace means the customer, provider, crew, and ops flows all need enough documentation and identity context to resolve problems responsibly.
Logged-in support paths should be used for live booking, billing, or account issues.
Evidence and intervention history may matter when disputes or refund reviews are raised.
The public explanation of terms should match what ops can actually support in practice.
trust_policy.terms_of_service.summary: The marketplace is meant to reduce friction without pretending every job is guaranteed, every route window is perfect, or every support issue resolves instantly.

Escalate only if the address is strategically adjacent to existing completed-work pockets or a verified provider already serves that exact block.
Do not promise availability outside the approved radius.
Do not convert a maybe into a booking just to test coverage.
If supply is thin, preserve route density over one-off expansion.
No provider can take the job cleanly
Searches show no verified provider match, or the available providers have no credible route window without forcing a bad operational fit.
Use provider outreach first, then either offer a realistic later window or close the loop instead of letting the request age in limbo.
Ops sends the timing reset or closeout.
Escalate when multiple open leads in the same service pocket are stalling so launch pricing, radius, or provider recruiting can be adjusted intentionally.
Do not overbook a provider just to save a lead.
Avoid same-day promises when the route is already fragile.
Document whether the miss was coverage, timing, payout fit, or service mismatch.
ops_launch_playbook.service_disruption.s: When service risk is operational, communication should get clearer and earlier, not more improvisational.
ops_launch_playbook.service_disruption.w: Weather makes the planned route unrealistic
Heavy rain, unsafe conditions, or ground conditions make the scheduled job poor quality or operationally risky.
Reschedule before the crew is trapped in an impossible route. Use the support or booking reschedule flow and give the customer the next realistic window.
Ops or the provider lead owns the outbound update, but ops should confirm the fallback plan.
Escalate when weather is affecting multiple jobs in the same day so the route plan is reset once instead of one ticket at a time.
Do not push crews into low-quality service just to preserve the original slot.
Prefer an explicit later window over vague same-day language.
If the weather decision changes payout, note that before the visit is marked complete.
ops_launch_playbook.service_disruption.d: Crew is late or blocked in the field
The provider sends a late update, access is blocked, or the customer is not ready when the crew arrives.
Use the delay or issue update immediately, then decide whether the visit should continue, reschedule, or move into support before the route stalls further.
Provider lead sends the first field update; ops owns the final expectation reset if the issue persists.
Escalate when the same booking gets more than one operational reversal or when the field issue could become a refund or dispute risk.
Keep the next action explicit: continue, reschedule, or close out.
Do not leave the customer waiting on an unresolved 'we are checking' loop.
Capture the field note before support resolution starts.
ops_launch_playbook.attendance.title: No-shows and failed handoffs
ops_launch_playbook.attendance.summary: The first weeks of launch need sharper rules around who missed the handoff and how quickly the team closes the loop.
ops_launch_playbook.attendance.customer_: Customer no-show or property not ready
The crew cannot start because the customer is absent, access is not ready, or the property conditions prevent the agreed scope.
Log the booking exception immediately, notify the customer, and decide whether the visit should be rescheduled or routed into support for a final decision.
Provider lead initiates the field note; ops owns any follow-up that changes the booking outcome.
Escalate when the no-show could trigger a fee dispute, a service-quality complaint, or a same-day crew hole that affects later jobs.
Do not mark the booking complete just because the crew arrived.
Do not reopen the route without a confirmed new window.
If the customer contests the story, move it into support with evidence attached.
ops_launch_playbook.attendance.provider_: A provider confirms the job but later drops it, no-shows, or cannot cover the route without breaking service expectations.
Try curated fallback supply first. If no clean replacement exists, reset the customer expectation quickly instead of pretending coverage is still intact.
Ops owns the final customer explanation and recovery plan.
Escalate immediately when the provider failure exposes a repeat reliability problem or leaves a high-value recurring customer stranded.
Protect trust before short-term conversion numbers.
Record whether the failure was staffing, route pressure, or provider reliability.
If there is no safe fallback, say so early.
ops_launch_playbook.verification.title: Provider go-live standards
ops_launch_playbook.verification.summary: Verification should screen for launch readiness, not just profile completeness.
ops_launch_playbook.verification.approve: Provider is ready to go live
The business profile is coherent, the service categories match the launch plan, and the provider can credibly serve the launch area without stretching the route.
Approve only when ops is comfortable letting the provider appear in recommendation-first customer search today.
No customer communication needed yet; this is a supply-quality gate.
Escalate if the provider is strategically valuable but still unclear on service area, payout expectations, or reliability standards.
Verification is a launch-quality gate, not a courtesy approval.
Prefer fewer reliable providers over broad fragile supply.
If ops sends the provider back, the note should say exactly what needs to change.
